Let's evaluate the variable importance result. The comparison between Top MDA on high satisfaction and low satisfaction customers will help to understand what parameters matter to define their satisfaction level. Below is the comparison between high satisfaction and low satisfaction customers based on the top MDA value. The table below shows the top 3 parameters that matter to high satisfaction and low satisfaction customers. The table is divided into 3 categories, which are: Type of Travel, Class, and Customers Type.<br>
<br>

| **Parameters Top MDA**| **High Satisfaction** | **Low Satisfaction**       |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------|
| **Type of Travel**    | **Business**          | **Personal**               |
| Top 1                 | Online Boarding       | In-flight WiFi Service     |
| Top 2                 | Check-in Service      | Ease of Online Booking     |
| Top 3                 | Baggage Handling      | Flight Entertainment       |
| **Class**             | **Business**          | **Economy and Economy Plus** |
| Top 1                 | Online Boarding       | In-flight WiFi Service     |
| Top 2                 | Departure and Arrival Time Convenience    | Baggage Handling    |
| Top 3                 | Check in Service      | Ease of online booking     |
| **Customers Type**    | **Returning**             | **First time**                   |
| Top 1                 | Departure and Arrival Time Convenience| In flight wifi service     |
| Top 2                 | Online Boarding       | Baggage Handling           |
| Top 3                 | In flight wifi service | In flight service         |

<br>
The table above shows that the top 3 parameters that matter to high satisfaction customers are different from the low satisfaction customers.
<br>
**Overall Insight**
For high satisfaction, the recurring themes are efficiency, convenience, and timeliness. Business travel and returning customers emphasize this the most.
For low satisfaction, comfort, accessibility, and entertainment take precedence, especially for personal travel and first-time customers.<br>

**Let's take a look on each group**
For **Type of Travel**, high satisfaction is driven by business travelers who value efficiency and convenience, particularly through services like online boarding, check-in service, and baggage handling. In contrast, low satisfaction among personal travelers stems from a focus on comfort and accessibility, with preferences for in-flight WiFi service, ease of online booking, and flight entertainment.<br>

For **Class**, high satisfaction is prominent among Business Class customers who emphasize seamless travel experiences, prioritizing online boarding, departure and arrival time convenience, and check-in service. On the other hand, low satisfaction in Economy and Economy Plus passengers highlights their need for enjoyable and accessible features, such as in-flight WiFi service, baggage handling, and ease of online booking.<br>

For **Customer Type**, returning customers experience high satisfaction when services like departure and arrival time convenience, online boarding, and in-flight WiFi service cater to their need for smooth and timely travel. Meanwhile, low satisfaction among first-time customers arises from their focus on pleasant first-time experiences, valuing in-flight WiFi service, baggage handling, and in-flight service.<br>

## Logistic Regression <a name="3.3"></a>

Why Logistic Regression?

Since this project aims to predict between binary class values (satisfied and dissatisfied), logistic regression will be used for this classification task. This method also allows us to identify the impact of each variable to the likelihood of passenger satisfaction, as well as see the probability values associated. In this subchapter, we will discuss step-by-step our process of preparing the regression model as well as interpret our findings.


### Model Preparation <a name="3.3.1"></a>

Firstly, we will prepare the dataset by applying a train-test split of 70:30. We will use seed value to get replicable results.


```{r}
set.seed(46748756)

# Treat ordinal variables as numeric and exclude specified variables
data_numeric <- data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ scale(.) %>% as.numeric())) %>% # Normalize all numeric columns
  mutate(across(c(Ease.of.Online.Booking, Check.in.Service, Online.Boarding, 
                  Gate.Location, On.board.Service, Seat.Comfort, Leg.Room.Service, 
                  Cleanliness, Food.and.Drink, In.flight.Service, In.flight.Wifi.Service, 
                  In.flight.Entertainment, Departure.and.Arrival.Time.Convenience), 
                as.numeric)) %>% # Treat ordinal variables as numeric
  subset(select = -c(ID, Gender, Age, Customer.Type, Type.of.Travel, Flight.Distance, 
                     Age_Range, Distance_Group, Age.log, Flight.Distance.log.z, Age.log.z, 
                     Departure.Delay.Duration, Arrival.Delay.Duration, 
                     Arrival.Delay.Duration.log, Arrival.Delay.Duration.log.z, 
                     Departure.Delay.Duration.log, Departure.Delay.Duration.log.z)) # Exclude unnecessary columns

# Cleaning columns with zero scores that exist in small quantities
cols_to_clean <- c("On.board.Service", "Check.in.Service", "Seat.Comfort",
                   "In.flight.Service", "Gate.Location", "Cleanliness", 
                   "In.flight.Entertainment")

for (col in colnames(data_numeric)) {
  if (is.factor(data_numeric[[col]])) {
    data_numeric[[col]] <- droplevels(data_numeric[[col]])
  }
}

# Split the dataset into training and testing sets
proportion <- 0.7
split <- initial_split(data_numeric, prop = proportion)
training <- training(split)
testing <- testing(split)

# Encode Satisfaction as binary (0 = Neutral or Dissatisfied, 1 = Satisfied)
training$Satisfaction <- ifelse(training$Satisfaction == "Satisfied", 1, 0)
training$Satisfaction <- factor(training$Satisfaction, levels = c(0, 1))
testing$Satisfaction <- ifelse(testing$Satisfaction == "Satisfied", 1, 0)
testing$Satisfaction <- factor(testing$Satisfaction, levels = c(0, 1))

# Split the dataset by class
business_class_data <- training %>% filter(Class == "Business") %>% select(-Class)
economy_class_data <- training %>% filter(Class %in% c("Economy", "Economy Plus")) %>% select(-Class)

```

The code chunk above first converts all specified columns into factors, as logistic regression requires categorical predictors to be factors. Next we remove one row which contains zero column values, as this cannot be split into the training and testing datasets. Finally, the dataset is split and we extract the training and testing set.

### Training Logistic Regression Model <a name="3.3.2"></a>

Once we have determined the training and testing set, we will train the model in the code chunk below.

-   **`glm()`**: Fits a generalized linear model.

-   **`Satisfaction ~ .`**: Specifies the formula, where `Satisfaction` is the dependent variable, and all other variables in the `training` dataset are independent variables.

-   **`data = training`**: Uses the `training` dataset to train the model.

-   **`family = "binomial"`**: Specifies that the model is a logistic regression, as the dependent variable (`Satisfaction`) is binary.

```{r training_logreg}

# Using all data
model_log <- glm(Satisfaction ~., 
               data = training, family = "binomial")
summary(model_log)
```

```{r training_logreg_business}

# Using business class data
model_log_business <- glm(Satisfaction ~., 
               data = business_class_data, family = "binomial")
summary(model_log_business)
```

```{r training_logreg_economy}

# Using economy class data
model_log_economy <- glm(Satisfaction ~., 
               data = economy_class_data, family = "binomial")
summary(model_log_economy)
```

The results above show the relationship between the predictor variables and the target variables. We are interested in determining the significant predictors of the model. In the next subchapter, we will delve deeper into the interpretation of these results.

### Interpretation of the Model <a name="3.3.3"></a>

**Interpret the coefficient**

The code chunk below is used to calculate the exponentiated coefficients (also known as odds ratios) from the logistic regression model `model_log`.

```{r}
exp(coef(model_log))
```

```{r}
exp(coef(model_log_business))
```

```{r}
exp(coef(model_log_economy))
```

The odds ratio indicates how the odds of the target variable (e.g., `Satisfaction` being "Satisfied") change with a one-unit increase in the predictor variable, holding all other variables constant.

-   **Odds Ratio \> 1**: The predictor increases the odds of satisfaction.

-   **Odds Ratio \< 1**: The predictor decreases the odds of satisfaction.

-   **Odds Ratio = 1**: The predictor has no effect on satisfaction.

We find that strong positive predictors include returning customers, business travelers, ease of online booking, and older passengers. Meanwhile, negative predictors include economy class travelers, low rating of online boarding and delays.

**Visualize the coefficient**

Below we will visualize the magnitude of each predictor's effect on the target variable, along with their 95% confidence intervals. The X axis represents the coefficient estimates in log-odds, horizontal lines around each point represent the confidence intervals (at 95% level).

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=20}

coefs <- summary(model_log)$coefficients

coef_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(coefs),
  Estimate = coefs[, "Estimate"],
  StdError = coefs[, "Std. Error"],
  p_value = coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

# Remove intercept for clarity
coef_df <- coef_df[coef_df$Variable != "(Intercept)", ]

# Plot using ggplot2
ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Estimate), y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Estimate - 1.96 * StdError,
                    ymax = Estimate + 1.96 * StdError), width = 0.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Logistic Regression Coefficients (All Class)",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Coefficient Estimate (log-odds)") +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=20}

coefs <- summary(model_log_business)$coefficients

coef_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(coefs),
  Estimate = coefs[, "Estimate"],
  StdError = coefs[, "Std. Error"],
  p_value = coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

# Remove intercept for clarity
coef_df <- coef_df[coef_df$Variable != "(Intercept)", ]

# Plot using ggplot2

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Estimate), y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Estimate - 1.96 * StdError,
                    ymax = Estimate + 1.96 * StdError), width = 0.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Logistic Regression Coefficients (Business Class)",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Coefficient Estimate (log-odds)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=20}
coefs <- summary(model_log_economy)$coefficients
coef_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(coefs),
  Estimate = coefs[, "Estimate"],

)

# Plot using ggplot2
ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Estimate), y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Estimate - 1.96 * StdError,
                    ymax = Estimate + 1.96 * StdError), width = 0.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Logistic Regression Coefficients (Economy Class)",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Coefficient Estimate (log-odds)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpreting Z Value**

```{r}
model_summary_business <- summary(model_log_business)
model_summary_economy <- summary(model_log_economy)

# Extract z-values and convert to data frame
z_df_business <- data.frame(
  Variable_business = rownames(model_summary_business$coefficients),
  Z_value_business = model_summary_business$coefficients[, "z value"]
)

# Remove intercept
z_df_economy <- data.frame(
  Variable_economy = rownames(model_summary_economy$coefficients),
  Z_value_economy = model_summary_economy$coefficients[, "z value"]
)

# Remove intercept
z_df_business <- subset(z_df_business, Variable_business != "(Intercept)")
z_df_economy <- subset(z_df_economy, Variable_economy != "(Intercept)")
```

```{r  fig.width=10, fig.height=20}
# Combine the two dataframes into one for plotting
z_df_business$Group <- "Business Class"
z_df_economy$Group <- "Economy + Economy Plus"

# Rename columns for consistency
z_df_business <- z_df_business %>% rename(Variable = Variable_business, Z_value = Z_value_business)
z_df_economy <- z_df_economy %>% rename(Variable = Variable_economy, Z_value = Z_value_economy)

# Combine the dataframes
z_df_combined <- rbind(z_df_business, z_df_economy)


# Plot using ggplot2

ggplot(z_df_combined, aes(x = reorder(Variable, abs(Z_value)), y = Z_value, fill = Group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") + # Side-by-side bars for each group
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") + # 95% significance threshold
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Z-values from Logistic Regression by Class",
       x = "Predictor Variable",
       y = "Z-value (Wald Statistic)",
       fill = "Passenger Class") + # Add legend for the groups
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Business Class" = "steelblue", "Economy + Economy Plus" = "green"))
```

The Z**-**values represent the Wald statistics for each predictor in the logistic regression model. These values are used to test the null hypothesis that the coefficient for a predictor is equal to zero.

-   Positive Z-values indicate a **positive** relationship to the likelihood of satisfaction.

-   Negative Z-values indicate a **negative** relationship to the likelihood of satisfaction.

For a 95% confidence level, the threshold of a statistically significant Z-value is **\|Z\| \> 1.96** which is indicated by the dotted red line in the plot. We can see from the visualization above that the strongest negative predictor for business class is departure time and arrival convenience, while for economy class is ease of online booking. The strongest positive predictor for business class is online boarding, and for economy class it is in-flight WiFi. Next, we will evaluate the model.

**Model Evaluation** <a name="3.3.4"></a>

The first calculation method that we will use to evaluate the logistic regression model is the confusion matrix. It is is a table that describes the performance of a classification model by comparing the predicted values with the actual values. It provides insight into how well the model is performing and helps identify any misclassifications. The result will display how many variables are correctly predicted as true positive and true negative as well as wrongly classified as false positive and false negative. The confusion matrix also calculate the accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of the model. The accuracy is the proportion of true results (both true positives and true negatives) among the total number of cases examined. Sensitivity is the proportion of true positives that are correctly identified, while specificity is the proportion of true negatives that are correctly classified.

We will use the confusion matrix to evaluate all three models: All Class, Economy Class, and Business Class. The code chunks below will show the confusion matrix for each model.

All Class :
```{r}
all_testing <- testing
pred.test <- predict(model_log, newdata = testing, type = "response")

# Convert to class labels
pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.5, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
all_testing$Satisfaction <- ifelse(testing$Satisfaction == 1, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
all_testing$Satisfaction <- factor(all_testing$Satisfaction, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))
pred.test.result <- factor(pred.test.result, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))

confusionMatrix(pred.test.result, all_testing$Satisfaction)
```

The confusion matrix for combined class showed a relatively good result in all three aspects, with accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity are all well above 80%. We will now look at the confusion matrix for economy class and business class separately.

Economy Class : 
```{r}
economy_class_test <- testing %>% filter(Class %in% c("Economy", "Economy Plus")) %>% select(-Class)

pred.test <- predict(model_log_economy, newdata = economy_class_test, type = "response")

# Convert to class labels
pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.5, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
economy_class_test$Satisfaction <- ifelse(economy_class_test$Satisfaction == 1, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
economy_class_test$Satisfaction <- factor(economy_class_test$Satisfaction, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))
pred.test.result <- factor(pred.test.result, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))

confusionMatrix(pred.test.result, economy_class_test$Satisfaction)

```

Although the economy class predictor has a very high accuracy and specificity number, it suffers from questionable sensitivity performance with only slightly above 50% value. This means that the model struggles to correctly identify satisfied customers in the economy class, which resulted in a high number of false negatives. This can be a potential issue, because the model is currently not accurately capturing the satisfaction levels for a lot of economy class travelers.

For Business Class :

```{r}
business_class_test <- testing %>% filter(Class %in% c("Business")) %>% select(-Class)

pred.test <- predict(model_log_business, newdata = business_class_test, type = "response")

# Convert to class labels
pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.5, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
business_class_test$Satisfaction <- ifelse(business_class_test$Satisfaction == 1, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
business_class_test$Satisfaction <- factor(business_class_test$Satisfaction, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))
pred.test.result <- factor(pred.test.result, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))

confusionMatrix(pred.test.result, business_class_test$Satisfaction)

```

We can see that this model performs noticeably better than the economy class predictor, with accuracy number of 84.6% and sensitivity of 90.5%. However it still suffers from relatively low specificity (71.1%). This means that almost 30% rate of false positives, which is not an ideal situation.

**Interpret ROC and AUC**

Another quantified way to evaluate the model is to use the ROC curve and Area Under the Curve (AUC) value. The ROC curve is a graphical representation of the true positive rate (sensitivity) against the false positive rate (1 - specificity) at various threshold settings. AUC provides a single measure of overall model performance, with values ranging from 0 to 1. If the AUC value is closer to 1, the more accurate the model's prediction is. AUC value of 0.5 indicates that the model has no identified pattern of guessing, which is essentially the same as random guessing. Meanwhile, AUC value of 0 means that the model is completely wrong in its predictions.

We will now look at the ROC curve and AUC value for each of the three models: All Class, Economy Class, and Business Class.


```{r}
# Running the model for all data
all_testing <- testing
pred.test <- predict(model_log, newdata = testing, type = "response")

# ROC curve and AUC
roc_obj <- roc(testing$Satisfaction, pred.test)
plot(roc_obj, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curve")
auc(roc_obj)
```

The ROC curve of All Class aboves shows that the model quickly reaches the value close to 1 in its initial phase, which indicates that the model has a good accuracy number. This is confirmed by the AUC value of 0.91, a value that is close to 1 and considered a good model.

```{r}
# Running the model for economy data
economy_testing <- testing
pred.test <- predict(model_log_economy, newdata = economy_class_test, type = "response")

# ROC curve and AUC
roc_obj_economy <- roc(economy_class_test$Satisfaction, pred.test)
plot(roc_obj_economy, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curve")
auc(roc_obj_economy)
```

For Economy Class model, the ROC curve takes a slightly longer path before it reach the value close to 1. From the AUC value of 0.8448, we can see that this model is still a good model, but not as good as the All Class model. This is consistent by the confusion matrix result above, where the economy class model has a lower accuracy and specificity number than the All Class model.

```{r}

# Running the model for all data
business_testing <- testing
pred.test <- predict(model_log_business, newdata = business_class_test, type = "response")

# ROC curve and AUC
roc_obj_business <- roc(business_class_test$Satisfaction, pred.test)
plot(roc_obj_business, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curve")
auc(roc_obj_business)

```

The Business Class model ROC curve shows a very good performance, similar with the All Class model. With AUC value of 0.9182, it can be considered a very good model.

### Improving Model Performance

**Using significant variables only**

Before we try several methods to improve the performance, we will display the summary of All Class model to see the AIC value. AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) is a measure of the relative quality of a statistical model for a given dataset. It is used to compare different models and select the best one. The lower the AIC value, the better the model fits the data. In this case, we will use AIC to compare the performance of different models.

```{r}

summary(model_log)

```

Above we see that the AIC value is 70412. We will use this value as a baseline to compare base model performance to the improved model.

The first method that we use to try improving the model performance is by filtering out the non-significant variables. We will use the p-value to determine the significance of each variable. The p-value is a statistical measure that helps to determine the significance of results. In this case, we will use a threshold of 0.05, which means that we will only keep the variables with a p-value less than 0.05. This is a common threshold used in statistical analysis to determine whether a result is statistically significant.

p-value \< 0.05

```{r}
training_signif <- training %>% subset(select = -c(Departure.Delay, Arrival.Delay,
                                                  In.flight.Wifi.Service, Food.and.Drink, 
                                                  In.flight.Entertainment,
                                                  In.flight.service, Flight.Entertainment, 
                                                  Comfortability, Pre.flight.service 
                                                  ))

model_log_signif <- glm(Satisfaction ~., 
               data = training_signif, family = "binomial")

summary(model_log_signif)

```

We saw a slight increase in AIC value to 73568. Because the value is higher, it indicates that the model with filtered variables is actually not better than the base model for All Class model.

Next, we will evaluate the new model through the Confusion Matrix:

```{r}
pred.test <- predict(model_log_signif, newdata = testing, type = "response")

# Convert to class labels
pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.5, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
all_testing$Satisfaction <- ifelse(testing$Satisfaction == 1, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
all_testing$Satisfaction <- factor(all_testing$Satisfaction, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))
pred.test.result <- factor(pred.test.result, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))

confusionMatrix(pred.test.result, all_testing$Satisfaction)
```

From the result above, the accuracy and sensitivity of the model with filtered variables experience a noticeable drop in accuracy and sensitivity value, while the specificity value is essentially the same. Again, this shows that the new model is not better than the base model.

The last method we want to use is using the ANOVA test to compare the two models. The ANOVA test is a statistical method used to compare the means of two or more groups. In this case, we will use the ANOVA test to compare the performance of the base model and the model with filtered variables. The ANOVA test will help us determine whether there is a significant difference between the two models. This is to ensure that the base model is indeed better than the model with filtered variables as indicated from the summary function and confusion matrix.

ANOVA test :

```{r}
anova(model_log, model_log_signif, test="Chisq")
```

The ANOVA test result above shows that the p-value is very close to 0, which indicates that there is a significant difference between the two models. This means that the base model is indeed better than the model with filtered variables, confirming the result from summary function and the confusion matrix.

**Adjusting Threshold**

The second method that we will use to improve the model performance is by adjusting the threshold value. The default threshold value is 0.5, which means that if the predicted probability is greater than 0.5, the model will classify it as "Satisfied". However, we can adjust this threshold value to see if it improves the model performance. Based on the ROC curve, we can see that the optimal threshold value is actually around 0.475, not 0.5. 


```{r}
coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = "threshold")
```

Now, we will run the confusion matrix again of the base model using the new threshold value of 0.475.

```{r}
all_testing <- testing
pred.test <- predict(model_log, newdata = testing, type = "response")

# Convert to class labels

pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.5, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.475096, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
all_testing$Satisfaction <- ifelse(testing$Satisfaction == 1, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
all_testing$Satisfaction <- factor(all_testing$Satisfaction, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))
pred.test.result <- factor(pred.test.result, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))

confusionMatrix(pred.test.result, all_testing$Satisfaction)
```

The new threshold value indicates a slight increase in sensitivity value, while the specificity value decrease for about 1% than the previous model. Meanwhile, the accuracy score essentially stays the same. This shows that the new threshold value is not significantly better than the previous model.

**Dimensionality Reduction**

The last method that we will use to try improving the predictor model is by using PCA (Principal Component Analysis). PCA is a statistical technique used to reduce the dimensionality of a dataset while preserving as much variance as possible. It transforms the original variables into a new set of uncorrelated variables called principal components. The first few principal components capture most of the variance in the data, allowing us to reduce the number of variables while retaining important information. 

```{r}
training_pca <- training %>%
  select(-Satisfaction) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ if (all(!is.na(as.numeric(as.character(.x))))) 
    as.numeric(as.character(.x)) else .x)) %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  scale(center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

pca_results <- prcomp(training_pca)
summary(pca_results)
```

In this case, the PCA reached more than 90% of the variance with only 12 components. Now we can reduce the dimensionality of dataset and see if it improves the model performance.

```{r}
pca_data <- as.data.frame(pca_results$x[, 1:12])
pca_data$Satisfaction <- training$Satisfaction

model_log_pca <- glm(Satisfaction ~., 
               data = pca_data, family = "binomial")

summary(model_log_pca)
```

The summary of the PCA model shows that the AIC value is 9913.8, which is significantly lower than the base model AIC value of 70412. This indicates that the PCA model is better than the base model. 

```{r}

train_center <- attr(training_pca, "scaled:center")
train_scale  <- attr(training_pca, "scaled:scale")

# 1. Convert test data to numeric and scale
test_pca_scaled <- testing %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ if (all(!is.na(as.numeric(as.character(.x))))) 
    as.numeric(as.character(.x)) else NA_real_)) %>%  # forces fallback to numeric NA
  select(all_of(names(train_center))) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%  # ensures everything is numeric
  scale(center = train_center, scale = train_scale)

# 2. Apply PCA transformation
test_pca <- as.data.frame(predict(pca_results, newdata = test_pca_scaled)[, 1:12])

# 3. Add target variable
test_pca$Satisfaction <- testing$Satisfaction

# 4. Predict using the model trained on PCA components
pred.test <- predict(model_log_pca, newdata = test_pca, type = "response")

# Convert to class labels
pred.test.result <- ifelse(pred.test > 0.5, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
test_pca$Satisfaction <- ifelse(test_pca$Satisfaction == 1, "Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied")
test_pca$Satisfaction <- factor(test_pca$Satisfaction, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))
pred.test.result <- factor(pred.test.result, levels = c("Satisfied", "Neutral or Dissatisfied"))

confusionMatrix(pred.test.result, test_pca$Satisfaction)
```

Accuracy decrease using PCA

## Result Visualization <a name="4.1"></a>

What are the aspects of service that are important towards customer satisfaction?

```{r important_aspects_of_service}
# Extract coefficients from the logistic regression models
coefs_business <- summary(model_log_business)$coefficients
coefs_economy <- summary(model_log_economy)$coefficients
# Create data frames for plotting
coef_df_business <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(coefs_business),
  Estimate = coefs_business[, "Estimate"],
  Abs_Estimate = abs(coefs_business[, "Estimate"])
)
coef_df_economy <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(coefs_economy),
  Estimate = coefs_economy[, "Estimate"],
  Abs_Estimate = abs(coefs_economy[, "Estimate"])
)
# Remove the intercept for clarity
coef_df_business <- coef_df_business[coef_df_business$Variable != "(Intercept)", ]
coef_df_economy <- coef_df_economy[coef_df_economy$Variable != "(Intercept)", ]
# Select the top 5 most important predictors for each class
top_5_business <- coef_df_business[order(-coef_df_business$Abs_Estimate), ][1:5, ]
top_5_economy <- coef_df_economy[order(-coef_df_economy$Abs_Estimate), ][1:5, ]
# Plot the top 5 predictors for Business Class

ggplot(top_5_business, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Abs_Estimate), y = Estimate)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Most Important Predictors (Business Class)",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Coefficient Estimate (log-odds)") +
  theme_minimal()
# Plot the top 5 predictors for Economy Class
ggplot(top_5_economy, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Abs_Estimate), y = Estimate)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "tomato") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Most Important Predictors (Economy Class)",
       x = "Predictor",
       y = "Coefficient Estimate (log-odds)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Recommendation <a name="4.2"></a>

Based on the *classification model, the variable importance analysis, and log regression model**, we can derive several recommendations to enhance customer satisfaction. The insights gained from the analysis can be tailored to different customer segments, ensuring that the improvements align with their specific needs and preferences.<br>

1. **Type of Travel**:<br>
   - For business travelers, focus on optimizing efficiency and convenience. Improve online boarding processes, enhance check-in services, and ensure smooth baggage handling to meet their expectations.<br>
   - For personal travelers, prioritize comfort and user-friendly experiences. Invest in better in-flight WiFi, simplify online booking platforms, and enhance in-flight entertainment to increase satisfaction.<br>

2. **Class**:<br>
   - In Business Class, emphasize seamless and time-sensitive services. Strengthen online boarding systems, ensure timely departures and arrivals, and offer superior check-in experiences.<br>
   - For Economy and Economy Plus passengers, focus on accessible and enjoyable features. Improve in-flight WiFi reliability, streamline baggage handling processes, and simplify online booking procedures.<br>

3. **Customer Type**:<br>
   - For returning customers, continue focusing on convenience and timeliness. Enhance departure and arrival time management, refine online boarding, and maintain quality in-flight connectivity.<br>
   - For first-time customers, create a welcoming and hassle-free experience. Highlight in-flight WiFi, ensure effective baggage handling, and offer exceptional in-flight service to leave a positive impression.<br>

## Conclusion & Limitations <a name="4.4"></a>

**Conclusion**

Part 1 Project Background outlines our objective to predict whether future airline customers would be satisfied based on detailed aspects of the service they received, and to identify which service components most significantly influence satisfaction. To address this, we utilized the Airline Passenger Satisfaction dataset, consisting of 129,880 individual responses reflecting customer experiences across various service touchpoints.

Part 2 Data Exploration and Preparation involved gaining a deeper understanding of the data structure, relationships between variables, and the necessary steps for cleaning and transforming the data. This process ensured we could proceed with high-quality input for modeling. Important steps included handling missing values, treating outliers, creating meaningful feature groups (such as flight service categories), and transforming skewed variables. These efforts resulted in a dataset optimized for reliable analysis and insight extraction.

Part 3 Data Modeling focused on applying logistic regression and decision tree (C5.0) models to predict satisfaction and identify key influencing variables. Dimensionality reduction using PCA helped uncover underlying patterns, revealing components such as in-flight amenities, digital and booking experience, and flight punctuality. Both models demonstrated high predictive accuracy, with decision tree models capturing complex interactions and logistic regression offering interpretability of individual variable effects.

Part 4 Interpretation summarized the insights and provided actionable recommendations for stakeholders in the airline industry. The findings confirmed that in-flight service, seat comfort, cleanliness, food and drink, and on-board service are consistently the most impactful drivers of customer satisfaction. The hypothesis proposed in Part 1 is supported, highlighting that service quality—particularly during the flight itself—is central to satisfaction outcomes.

In conclusion, this analysis presents valuable insights for airline service providers seeking to enhance customer experience. By prioritizing core service components and operational reliability, airlines can not only improve satisfaction levels but also build stronger customer loyalty in a highly competitive market.
